content.text:
Operator
Thank you for standing by, and welcome to Enterprise Products Partners L.P.'s Q4 2024 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speaker presentation, there will be a question and answer. For this session, you will need to press star one. You may press star one-one again. I would now like to hand the call over to Libby Strait, Senior Director of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.
Libby Strait
Senior Director of Investor Relations, Enterprise Products Partners
Good morning and welcome to the Enterprise Products Partners Conference Call to Discuss Q4 2024 Earnings. Our speakers today will be Co-Chief Executive Officers of Enterprise's general partner, Jim Teague and Randy Fowler. Other members of our senior management team are also in attendance for the call today. During this call, we will make forward-looking statements within the meaning of Section 21E of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 based on the beliefs of the company, as well as assumptions made by and information currently available to Enterprise's management team.
Although management believes that the expectations reflected in such forward-looking statements are reasonable, it can give no assurance that such expectations will prove to be correct. Please refer to our latest filings with the SEC for a list of factors that may cause actual results to differ materially from those in the forward-looking statements made during this call. With that, I'll turn it over to Jim.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Thank you, Libby. I want to just go through some bullet points to highlight some of the things we achieved in 2024, and a few of the things we expect to do this year. First of all, 2024 EBITDA of $9.9 billion. Randy, it reminds me of a line in a Frankie Valli song, so close, so close, and yet so far. We had $7.8 billion of DCF. We had 1.7x coverage. $3.2 billion of retained DCF. Chris, I thought that was a record, but it's not. But it's close. 12 financial records, 16 operational records. During 2024, we moved 12.9MMbpd of oil equivalent a day. In Q4, we moved 13.6MMbpd of oil equivalent per day.
In Q4, we loaded out for export 2.1MMbpd of liquid hydrocarbons against our ton commitments of 2.5MMbpd. During 2024 and early 2025, we completed two processing plants in the Permian. We purchased Piñon, acquired the L.P. interest in our Midland-to-ECHO 1 crude oil pipeline, and the L.P. interest in our seventh and eighth fractionators. For 2025, we'll add two gas processing plants in the Permian. We'll add the Bahia NGL Pipeline, Frac 14, the first phase of our NGL export on the Neches River, and expansions of our ethane and ethylene terminal at Morgan's Point. That list almost needs to pause and take a breath. We get a lot of questions on SPOT. I want to give you a status report of where we are with SPOT.
I believe that SPOT should be the poster child for the need for permit reform. By law, the record of decisions should be issued in 356 days, and you can have clock stoppages on top of that. Frankly, I thought 356 was a typo, but it wasn't. Although it took over five years to get the SPOT license, including almost four years to get the record of decision and a year and a half to get the license to construct. Our initial application was 13,000 pages. I thought that was ridiculous, but by the time we completed the process, our final submission was over 30,000 pages. We addressed over 80,000 comments over two comment periods, predominantly from NGOs. One NGO's comment was 60 pages long. We had to answer a ton of questions.
One of my favorites was from a lady from Murad, asking how we plan to mow the right of way. She was concerned that field mice be protected from hawks. The process we went through due to federal bureaucracy pushed us beyond a drop-dead date that allowed our anchor customer to opt out of their contract, which they did. Granted, a lot has changed since we entered our SPOT application in January 2019. When we started that application, it was assumed that the majority of crude exports would go to Asia on VLCCs. A lot of forecasters were predicting by 2024, the US would be exporting between 7MMbpd and 8MMbpd Instead, we're exporting around 4MMbpd
Follow that with Russia invading Ukraine, which has resulted in the amount of crude oil export out of the US to Europe to have doubled to over 2MMbpd and that will grow more. That move to Europe can be done on an Aframax or a Suezmax. Today, we have not gotten enough traction in commercializing SPOT, though we continue to promote SPOT as we are the only company with a license to construct. We did a lot of research around cost, and our data shows that the cost to load on our SPOT project are always much lower than multi-vessel lightered VLCCs, and have a lower all-in cost than 50% of single vessel lightered VLCCs, and are competitive with the best 50% single vessel lightered VLCCs. However, in order to build SPOT, we know what we need in volumes, fees, and terms.
We're not gonna establish a drop-dead date, but if we can't achieve these within a reasonable amount of time, we will move on. This is not a build-it-and-they-will-come project. Regardless, Enterprise remains laser-focused on growing our exports. As I said earlier, we currently have expansion projects on the Neches River in Beaumont, at Morgan's Point on the Ship Channel, and our main terminal on the Ship Channel. We exported over 70 million barrels of hydrocarbons in December, and our goal is that we will export over 100 million barrels of hydrocarbons a month by 2027. We recently contracted, we got another ethane uptake customer in Asia, this one with a plant in Vietnam. We are working with numerous other customers around the world on hydrocarbon supply agreements.
In the last 24 months, we've visited over 25 cities to sell US hydrocarbons. Some we visited multiple times. I know I've been in Mumbai at least four times. Someone from Enterprise is almost always in Asia or Europe, and no one even comes close to having the history and experience that we have. Think about it, we built our first LPG import terminal in 1983 and our first export terminal in 1999. We've been active in the international market for over 40 years. On a personal note, while I was at Dow, the first cargo of imported propane that I ever purchased went through the Enterprise terminal. Our total term commitments at our docks today exceed 2.5MMbpd, and that's hydrocarbons, ethylene to crude oil.
We're 3/4 of the way to reaching our goal of 100 million barrels a month. With that, I'll turn it over to Randy.
Randy Fowler
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Okay. Thank you, Jim, and good morning to everyone on the call. Starting with Q4 income statement items, net income attributable to common unit holders for Q4 2024 was $1.6 billion or $0.74 per common unit on a fully diluted basis. This is a 3% increase compared to $1.6 billion or $0.72 per unit for the same quarter in 2023. Adjusted cash flow from operations, which is cash flow from operating activities before changes in working capital, increased 4% to $2.3 billion for Q4. This compares to $2.2 billion for Q4 2023.
We declared a distribution of 53.5 per common unit for Q4 2024, which is a 4% increase over the distribution declared for Q4 2023. The distribution will be paid 4 February 2025 to common unit holders of record as of the close of business on 31 January 2025. In Q4, the partnership purchased approximately 2.1 million common units off the open market for $63 million. Total purchases for 2024 were $219 million, or approximately 7.6 million Enterprise common units, bringing total purchases under our buyback program to approximately $1.1 billion.
In addition to buybacks, our distribution reinvestment plan and employee unit purchase plan purchased a combined 6.5 million common units on the open market for $188 million in 2024. This includes 1.6 million common units for $48 million during Q4 of 2024. Of note, almost half of our employees participate in the employee unit purchase plan. For 2024, Enterprise paid out approximately $4.6 billion in cash distributions to limited partners. Combined with the $219 million of common unit repurchases over the same period, Enterprise's total capital return of $4.8 billion resulted in a payout ratio of 55%.
Since our IPO in 1998, we have returned approximately $56 billion to unitholders in the form of distributions and buybacks while building one of the largest energy infrastructure networks in North America. Total capital investments in Q4 2024 were $2 billion, which includes $946 million for growth capital projects, $949 million for the acquisition of Piñon Midstream, and $113 million of sustaining capital expenditures. Capital investments for the full year of 2024 were $5.5 billion, which includes $3.9 billion for organic growth capital projects, the $945 million for Piñon, and $667 million for sustaining capital expenditures. As mentioned in last quarter's earnings call, we have received noteworthy support from our producer customers following the Piñon acquisition.
For that reason, we are fine-tuning our 2025 estimated growth capital expenditures range to $4 to 4.5 billion to include new opportunities in sour gas gathering and treating projects, as well as additional natural gas gathering and compression projects in the Delaware Basin. Our expected range of growth capital expenditures for 2026 remains unchanged at $2 to 2.5 billion. We expect 2025 sustaining capital expenditures will be approximately $525 million, which includes a planned turnaround at our octane enhancement plant. Moving to capitalization, our total debt principal outstanding was approximately $32.2 billion as of 31 December 2024. Assuming the final maturity date for our hybrids, the weighted average life of our debt portfolio was approximately 18 years.
Our weighted average cost of debt was 4.7%, and approximately 98% of our debt was fixed rate. Our consolidated liquidity was approximately $4.8 billion at the end of the year, including availability under our credit facilities and unrestricted cash on hand. Our Adjusted EBITDA was $2.6 billion for Q4 and, as Jim mentioned, $9.9 billion for 2024. We ended the year with a consolidated leverage ratio of 3.1x on a net basis after adjusting debt for the partial equity credit treatment of our hybrid debt and reduced by the partnership's unrestricted cash on hand. Our leverage target remains 3x ±0.25, so in the range of 2.75 to 3.25. With that, Libby, I think we can open up for questions.
Libby Strait
Senior Director of Investor Relations, Enterprise Products Partners
Thank you, Randy. Operator, we are ready to open up the call for questions.
Operator
Thank you. As a reminder, to ask a question, you will need to press star one one on your telephone. To remove yourself from the queue, you may press star one one again. Please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up or two questions to allow everyone the opportunity to participate. Please stand by while we compile the Q&A roster. Our first question comes from the line of Spiro Dounis of Citi. Your question please, Spiro.
Spiro Dounis
Director of Equity Research, Citi
Thanks, operator. Morning, everybody. First question, maybe just go to the outlook for 2025. I know you guys don't provide guidance, but we just got results, the way you closed the year seemed like it was pretty strong. Just curious, two-part question here. Any reason that that's not a good baseline to sort of run rate as we think about 2025? And then if you could, maybe just outline some of the bigger drivers of growth this year.
Randy Fowler
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Yeah, Spiro, you know, I'll go back to what we said on our investor day call a year ago, that really we think near term, we've got the potential for, call it, mid-single digit cash flow growth over the near to intermediate term. I think that's sort of our view going into 2025. Jim mentioned the number of projects that we have coming on. Most of them, the larger ones for sure, come on later in the year.
You know, we'll see some of that growth on the second half of the year. you know, 2025 is setting up a strong year, especially when you come in and just look at industry fundamentals.
Spiro Dounis
Director of Equity Research, Citi
Great. That's helpful. Thanks, Randy. Second question, just to go back to SPOT. So I know you're not providing a drop-dead date to get that facility FID-ed, but two parts here once again. Does it seem less likely or unlikely at this point that a 2025 FID is possible? And you also mentioned being the only one licensed. Just curious, can you just talk about license expiration timing, what that looks like, and what it would take to renew it if you don't FID, let's call it within two years?
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Yeah. I think we've renewed one permit, Bob?
Bob Sanders
EVP of Asset Optimization, Enterprise Products Partners
Yeah, we renewed the air permit, right, Graham, to 2028?
Graham Bacon
EVP and COO, Enterprise Products Partners
Yeah. We're not that worried about renewing permits if we need to.
Spiro Dounis
Director of Equity Research, Citi
Okay. Does it seem like a 25 FID based on customer feedback at this point, may be less likely?
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
I'm not gonna admit to that.
Spiro Dounis
Director of Equity Research, Citi
Okay. Tried to get you. All good. I appreciate the color here. I'll leave it there. Thank you, guys.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Theresa Chen of Barclays. Please go ahead, Theresa.
Theresa Chen
Senior Analyst, Barclays
Thank you for taking my questions. Follow-up to the cadence of earnings growth in 2025. Can you help us think about the path to recovery for the Petchem segment? What are the puts and takes there? As far as operations and utilization goes for the larger, you know, the newer projects, how's that going at this point?
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
I think we've got to run the PDHs. That's one thing from our perspective, and we will. From a petrochemical market perspective, I don't think Chris is here, but. Oh, there he is. But it looks pretty bad right now, doesn't it, Chris?
Chris D'Anna
SVP of Petrochemicals, Enterprise Products Partners
Yeah. I think what we're hearing from most of our customers domestically is they're seeing moderate improvement from last year, and they're not expecting anything much bigger. Globally, the market is oversupplied, so that's the headwind there.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Here's. Who was it? Theresa?
Bob Sanders
EVP of Asset Optimization, Enterprise Products Partners
Mm-hmm.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Yeah, Theresa. This is Jim. What I see is we are signing. We just signed recently within the last two or three weeks, Tug, a contract with a Southeast Asian petrochemical company for a sizable ethane contract. I think we'll be back in Southeast Asia for another one. We, the other thing that I wouldn't be surprised at is ethane feedstock to crackers in other parts of the world is advantaged to naphtha. It wouldn't surprise me, and help me, Chris, to see crackers shut down in other parts of the world and ethylene exports beginning to fill that void.
Chris D'Anna
SVP of Petrochemicals, Enterprise Products Partners
Yeah, I mean, we're already seeing some of that. That helps not only our ethylene, but it also helps the propylene markets 'cause those naphtha crackers in the rest of the world also do make some amount of propylene. That'll help rationalization.
Theresa Chen
Senior Analyst, Barclays
Interesting. Thank you so much. Then on the LPG side, following a competitor announcement of a new export project in Galveston Bay today, how do you think about, you know, the potential change to export economics to competitive economics within the region?
Brent Secrest
EVP and Chief Commercial Officer, Enterprise Products Partners
Teresa, this is Brent. As you see capacity come online, and there's industry capacity come online this year, we'll have some in the back half of this year as well, and then a larger expansion for next year. Right now, the dock FOB values are pretty healthy. Obviously, as this capacity comes online, those will start to become eroded. When you look at our capital for expansion, it's less than a third of what a greenfield expansion is. You know, we'll see. I didn't listen to the call, but you know, that's in terms of when we run the numbers, that's a little bit of a challenging project.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Theresa, this is Jim. We're not gonna give up our LPG export franchise. We'll replace when we're preferable to our customers than anyone.
Theresa Chen
Senior Analyst, Barclays
Understood. Nor would I expect you to give anything up, Jim. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Jean Ann Salisbury of BofA. Your question please, Jean Ann.
Jean Ann Salisbury
Managing Director, BofA
Hi. Good morning. Can you talk about how you see the size of the eventual prize for being able to handle sour gas in the Permian? Do you expect sour gas to grow much faster as a share, or is it mainly a strategy to be able to have a broader customer offering and get more customers?
Natalie Gayden
SVP of Natural Gas Assets, Enterprise Products Partners
Hey, Jean Ann, this is Natalie. I don't think anything's gonna be fast. However, we are permitting a third AGI well, or we're in the front of it. We're also expanding the two AGI wells there. We'll build our fourth train, and then we have our eyes on a fifth train. I don't know how quickly, but I think we'll. It does give us a new asset base to be able to expand the integrated value chain to the upstream side.
Jean Ann Salisbury
Managing Director, BofA
Okay, that makes sense. As a follow-up, can you just kind of talk about how you expect your flex NGL exports to ramp as they come online, roughly how much in ethane versus propane service to start?
Tug Hanley
SVP of Hydrocarbon Marketing, Enterprise Products Partners
Hi, Jean Ann. This is Tug Hanley here. Yeah, on the ethane side, we're fully contracted on our base capacity of 540,000 barrels a day. We're in the process of we've identified low cost expansion debottlenecking projects, and we're well into contracting that additional capacity. If you think about how that's gonna play out, we're waiting on VLEC, the ships to get delivered. As those ships continue to get delivered and ramp our ethane exports at our Neches River terminal, that timing coincides with our ship channel expansion around 300,000 barrels a day. Long term, we expect it to be ethane at Neches, and we'll have our ship channel expansion to tackle that. We're continuing to see robust demand on the ethane exports.
As Brent alluded to, we have a great brownfield expansion opportunities across all three of our export terminals. Then when our expansion comes on for LPGs, we're 85% contracted on LPGs.
Jean Ann Salisbury
Managing Director, BofA
Well, great. That's great color. I'll leave it there. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Michael Blum of Wells Fargo. Your question, please, Michael.
Michael Blum
Equity Analyst, Wells Fargo
Thank you. Good morning, everyone. Appreciate the slide and the comments on capital allocation. I wanted to ask you about buybacks specifically. Just if you're thinking about buybacks any differently as a component of capital return, should we expect the cadence we've seen the last couple of years to be consistent going forward or any change there?
Randy Fowler
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Yeah. Michael, good morning. If we sort of come in and carry that theme as far as the potential for cash flow growth to be mid-single digits. You know, Jim mentioned earlier that we had $3.2 billion of excess distributable cash flow in 2024. If you take that forward a couple of years to 2026, that probably puts you in the neighborhood of $3.5 to 3.6 billion of excess DCF. If we're up at the upper end of our growth CapEx range of $2.5 billion, that leaves you about $1.1 billion of excess DCF after fully funding your growth CapEx with excess DCF that's left over for buybacks and debt retirement.
You know, where our leverage target, again, is the range 2.75 to 3.25. Our midpoint's three. That's about where our leverage is today. You know, I think we'll have a lot more flexibility to do buybacks and maybe a little bit of debt retirement once we get out to 2026.
Michael Blum
Equity Analyst, Wells Fargo
Thanks for that, Randy. Appreciate it. Then just wanted to ask about as we head here into 2025, the M&A landscape, how active, you know, what's out there for you, and do you expect this to be an active year for Enterprise? Thanks.
Randy Fowler
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Yeah. You know, 2024 was a pretty active year and you know we've looked at virtually every asset package that came across. And again, Piñon was the most attractive to us and we executed on that. You know, we do see some additional asset packages, or we think we'll see some later in the year, and we'll take a hard look at those and you know see what fits well in our system. Public company M&A is a little bit harder to do, especially if your end goal is to drive cash flow per share, cash flow per unit growth. Public M&A can be a little on the problematic side. Don't see as much value as we do with asset purchases. We'll take a look at those.
Michael Blum
Equity Analyst, Wells Fargo
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Neal Dingmann of Truist Securities. Your question please, Neil.
Neal Dingmann
Managing Director, Truist Securities
Morning. Thanks for the time. My first question, guys, just on GOM. I'm just wondering, looks like that the processing spread and others have stayed, or I guess they were pretty stable for the remainder of last year. Are you expecting more of that this year? Or, you know, maybe just talk about the activity there.
Bob Sanders
EVP of Asset Optimization, Enterprise Products Partners
I mean, I think in terms of the forward curve, Neal, I think we think that spread's gonna be there. It's probably more when you look at Waha, it's a function of Waha gas price. I would probably think ethane's fairly stable for this year. It's probably gonna escalate a little bit, but in terms of the processing spread in our system and the recovery of ethane, it's probably more of a function of the Waha gas price.
Neal Dingmann
Managing Director, Truist Securities
Got it. Okay. Just one forward. Love to hear just on prospects of now where we sit on the macro side. I'm just wondering based on, you know, how you all are looking at it. You've talked about M&A now today. Is that predicated on, you know, what you're thinking on the macro on both the oil and the gas side? I just wanted to hear kind of what you're thinking for the remainder of the year on the macro commodity side.
Randy Fowler
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Hey, Neal, would you mind repeating that?
Neal Dingmann
Managing Director, Truist Securities
Yeah. You know, Randy, you laid out kind of, you know, I know you guys are active on the M&A side. I'm just wondering, is this predicated? I'd love to hear.
You guys always give a pretty good forecast on what you're thinking the commodity-wise, both gas, you know, I'd say gas, NGLs, and oil. I'm just wondering, are you expecting a bit of a ramp commodity-wise for the remainder of the year? I guess I'm asking is, you know, is M&A predicated on this?
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
I don't know that M&A is predicated on it, but you're talking a ramp in price or ramp in production?
Neal Dingmann
Managing Director, Truist Securities
Price. Yeah, I'm just trying to figure out what you all are thinking for price in the remainder of the year.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
For price, if we start with oil, it's been range-bound, not at really bad prices, quite frankly. It's really been quite range-bound, not just for the last year, but even longer than that. Our belief is that, the OPEC+ continues to be very focused on that. They don't want prices too high, and they don't want them too low. I don't know what changes that landscape. Right now, there's a lot of discussion about will we move into a, for lack of a better term, quote-unquote, drill, baby, drill scenario. All signs are that we will not, that it'll be, you know, call it slow and steady from very large numbers already. That said, we continue to see that rich natural gas production, just sticking to the Permian, continues to exceed our expectations.
We will be reforecasting and publishing new forecast probably sometime in Q2. We're working on it now. I'll say, Neal, I wouldn't be surprised if our natural gas liquids forecast in the Permian specifically is not up again from the prior one, but give us some time to work through it.
Neal Dingmann
Managing Director, Truist Securities
That's what I was after.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
You know, Brent's pointed to the natural gas equation. It's somewhat weather-related. Waha is very much what pipes can you count on running related. That matters a lot to us. There you have that.
Neal Dingmann
Managing Director, Truist Securities
Perfect. Thank you.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Last but not least, we're pretty constructive on natural gas long term, just because of what we see from the demand standpoint for LNG and for power.
Neal Dingmann
Managing Director, Truist Securities
Okay.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Jeremy Tonet of J.P. Morgan Securities. Please go ahead, Jeremy.
Jeremy Tonet
Executive Director and Research Analyst, J.P. Morgan Securities
Hi, good morning.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Good morning.
Jeremy Tonet
Executive Director and Research Analyst, J.P. Morgan Securities
Just wanted to start off, I guess, any updated thoughts out of DC, just wondering, you know, in the Trump administration, imagine permitting might be easier, also talking about energy emergency and how that could impact, you know, permitting overall. Just wondering what you hear coming out of DC, anything different? Could that impact, I guess, your, you know, growth strategy going forward?
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Permit reform would be nice, but I got to see it to believe it, frankly.
Jeremy Tonet
Executive Director and Research Analyst, J.P. Morgan Securities
Got anything else out of DC on your radar right now or just kind of business as usual?
Randy Fowler
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Jeremy, you know, on the permit reform, just seems like that's gonna take some time and pretty involved. You know, the other thing is just what the administration is looking to do as far as from a tax package and extend some of these provisions at sunset at the end of 2025 to get extended. Thus far, really no surprises from where we were, frankly, right after the election. It seems like the administration and Congress are following through with what they were talking about during the election cycle and right after the election.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
You know, Jeremy, the lack of permanent reform seems to make what we have in the ground a heck of a lot more valuable.
Jeremy Tonet
Executive Director and Research Analyst, J.P. Morgan Securities
Got it. Yeah, no, absolutely. Just wanted to touch base real quick on the PDH facilities one and two. Where are the current, I guess, operating run rates and where do you see them going over the course of 25 and kind of hitting a normalized level?
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
You wanna hit it, Graham?
Graham Bacon
EVP and COO, Enterprise Products Partners
Yes, Jim. This is Graham. You know, right now we're looking to increase the run rates of the PDHs. Obviously, they haven't met our expectations. Currently, we're working through a mechanical issue on PDH 1, but coming out of our turnaround last year, it really ran pretty well. We had a minor blip we're working through right now, but expect a, you know, sustained run rate there. PDH 2, we're working through a design issue with our licensor that has the rates currently limited. We expect to get that resolved and, you know, our long-term target is to have those operating in the upper 90% of utilization.
Jeremy Tonet
Executive Director and Research Analyst, J.P. Morgan Securities
Okay. Got it. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of John Mackay of Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead, John.
John Mackay
VP of Equity Research, Goldman Sachs
Hey, good morning. Thanks for the time. I wanna stay on some of the policy stuff. We've obviously seen a lot of different headlines on the tariff front, but we had some kind of retaliatory tariffs from China overnight, I guess. So far from China, they're not on the NGL front, but I guess I'd just be curious to hear your takes overall on any of these energy tariffs, how you think about that in the context of your export footprint. Thank you.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
China imports, I think we have one contract with one Chinese company on propane. Is that right, Tug?
Tug Hanley
SVP of Hydrocarbon Marketing, Enterprise Products Partners
That's right. That's right.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Yeah, a lot of propane out of the US goes to China for their PDH plants, Tug. They've got a lot of PDH plants, and they don't have any propane, so I don't see it affecting that. We have ethane contracts with two customers, and those crackers can only use ethane, Tug.
Tug Hanley
SVP of Hydrocarbon Marketing, Enterprise Products Partners
Right.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
They don't have any ethane. From an NGL perspective, I'm not worried. Now that's most of what we have that go on the LPG that goes to China goes through trading companies. We're getting interest in places like Southeast Asia, where we're gonna have two contracts before it's all said and done. We're expanding another contract in Asia by 40,000 barrels a day. We have a huge contract in Europe. Tug was a little modest when he says 540,000. I think where we will end up on ethane is 600,000. Oh, he's pointing higher. Then I think on I think 85% LPG, I think we'll contract that out before it's all said and done.
John Mackay
VP of Equity Research, Goldman Sachs
I appreciate all that. Thank you. Maybe just a follow-up. I wanted to ask about the NGL pipeline side volume. If we're just looking year-over-year, I know there's always a little bit of noise, but, you know, volumes were up a lot. Margin itself wasn't up a ton. You guys called out some higher costs. I'd just be curious your take on kind of NGL pipe margins going from here, how to think about those, you know, that extra OpEx side, and then maybe comment on this in the context of broader NGL pipe competition. Thanks.
Justin Kleiderer
SVP of Pipelines and Terminals, Enterprise Products Partners
Yeah, this is Justin. A few things going on on the volume side, so let's cover that. Significant, you know, walk-up volume, which incorporates a lot of our purity movements along with the trajectory that we see on just overall Y-grade growth. You're seeing some a big quarterly step-up as a function of some of those month-to-month movements on the purity side. We are continuing to see that nice ramp of Y-grade volumes trending in the right direction. On the GOM side, when you look at the GOM side, it's one thing to note that while Permian Y-grade rates stay in the reinvestment economic range, as we build out the Bahia, a lot of what changes associated to Rockies flows and those Rockies tariffs are significantly higher.
Sometimes that can, when you look at this volume and GOM perspective, make the fee otherwise skew the fee. Changes in our Rockies flows can sometimes make the per unit GOM otherwise more skewed than what you would anticipate. All in all, though, the growth that we're seeing in the Permian continues to support reinvestment economics on the wide grade side.
John Mackay
VP of Equity Research, Goldman Sachs
Sorry, just on the context of kind of competition from new pipes coming in, how are you feeling about that?
Justin Kleiderer
SVP of Pipelines and Terminals, Enterprise Products Partners
Yeah, you know, we still like our platform. We're still growing our G&P footprint. I'd say, when you look at in service of Bahia in Q4, you know, we're quickly right behind that going to convert Seminole back to crude service. We've guided to that in prior calls. When you take that into account, you know, going into 2026, we'd expect Bahia to be 60% full with more coming behind it as we continue to ramp. We still feel like our platform gives us a pathway to being full over the coming years.
John Mackay
VP of Equity Research, Goldman Sachs
All right. That's clear. Appreciate the time. Thanks so much.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of AJ O'Donnell of TPH. Your question, please, AJ.
AJ O'Donnell
Director of Equity Research, TPH
Yeah. Thanks. Good morning, everyone. I was just hoping maybe we could start on NGL marketing. There was some notable strength there quarter-over-quarter. I was just wondering if you could expand a little bit on, you know, the prospects for 2025, you know, in light of commodity price movements and maybe the potential to offset any lower margins from natural gas marketing as a result of higher Waha spreads.
Randy Fowler
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Yeah, I mean, it's a function. We had some higher FOB values across our dock on the LPG side, but the bottom line is, as volatility presents itself, and the market will be there to monetize it, and we continue to do that, and those opportunities continue to present themselves.
AJ O’Donnell
Director of Equity Research, TPH
Okay. Thanks for that. Maybe one more, you know, on data centers. We saw the Stargate announcement, you know, and I'm just curious. I know you guys have some intrastate lines in the area. Is there any capacity on your Texas intrastate system to be able to feed that project?
Natalie Gayden
SVP of Natural Gas Assets, Enterprise Products Partners
We still have the capacity on both of our. It just depends on where the project is. Just to give you some perspective of how much data center demand is out there, we've got probably 20 data center projects in the queue on the Texas side. It equates to over two BCF a day of demand. We believe only probably 15% of those projects are showing signs of progress. On the power plant side, which may feed data centers, if you believe it's just power from those, we're looking at probably 15 potential projects around 1.2 BCF a day, and maybe 50% of those are real. Where depends on where the data center project is, and it stems all the way from Dallas to San Antonio.
If our lines are closed, we're gonna take the opportunity to serve the data centers where it makes sense.
AJ O’Donnell
Director of Equity Research, TPH
Okay. Great. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Brandon Blossman of Scotiabank. Your question please, Brandon.
Brandon Blossman
Analyst, Scotiabank
Hi. Thanks for taking the questions. If we could go back to the volumes side and the volumes outperformance this quarter, just wondering how sticky those volumes are and kinda how you see that progressing throughout 2025.
Randy Fowler
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Yeah, Brandon, I think if you come in, I mean that's really just the growth at the wellhead, especially the growth at the Permian and really the benefit of a value chain. It's flowing into our gas processing plants. Those liquids out of the processing plants flow into our downstream pipelines through our fractionators all the way to the dock. What is that theme, wellhead to water? I think that's pretty much what you're seeing across our system.
Brandon Blossman
Analyst, Scotiabank
Awesome. Thank you. If we could just quickly go back to the pet chem side, you know, and on the margin front. You guys had previously discussed the PDH plants contributing, I think it was roughly $200 million a year in EBITDA whenever they're running as they should. Could you just talk about what margins were baked into that $200 million number and how those compare to what you're currently seeing?
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Well, the margins haven't changed 'cause it's a formulaic price. Isn't that right, Chris?
Chris D'Anna
SVP of Petrochemicals, Enterprise Products Partners
Yeah, the way our PDH contracts are set up, they're all toll-based, so it's cost plus. It's really just a function of utilization rates.
Randy Fowler
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
Really what we were talking about was, I think when we looked at where earnings were in 2024, we see the potential for the PDHs to contribute an incremental $200 million in 2025.
Brandon Blossman
Analyst, Scotiabank
Got it. Okay. Thank you.

Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Manav Gupta of UBS. Please go ahead, Manav.
Manav Gupta
Analyst, UBS
Good morning. My quick question here is any update on the Morgan's Point flex expansion that you can provide?

As far as an update on where we are with.

The Morgan's Point flex train?
Speaker 19
Yes.

Yeah, this is Chris D'Anna. We finished the construction at the end of December of last year, so it's in service and ready to serve. Analyst, UBS
The second one is more on the Haynesville side. Do you still see that as a growth basin, and are you looking at growth opportunities coming out of the Haynesville Basin?

SVP of Natural Gas Assets, Enterprise Products Partners
Haynesville is a growing basin, although rig counts wouldn't show that to be true. We have seen some growth in our portfolio, and this is from new acreage developments that producers are hitting. However, I don't know that the Haynesville has truly grown over the last year. I would say the opposite. Over the next year, I think we do see some growth potential, but again, gas price drives that story.
Manav Gupta
Analyst, UBS
Thank you so much.
Randy Fowler
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners
We'll be updating our Haynesville forecast, at least for its potential when we have better forecast in Q2.
Jim Teague

What it's doing and what its potential is is key.
Randy Fowler

Operator
Thank you for standing by. Welcome to Enterprise Products Partners L.P.'s Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speaker presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question during the session, you will need to press star one one on your telephone. To remove yourself from the queue, you may press star one one again. I would now like to hand the call over to Libby Strait, Senior Director of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.
Libby Strait
Senior Director of Investor Relations, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Good morning and welcome to the Enterprise Products Partners conference call to discuss Q2 2024 earnings. Our speakers today will be Co-Chief Executive Officers of Enterprise's General Partner, Jim Teague and Randy Fowler. Other members of our senior management team are also in attendance for the call today. During this call, we will make forward-looking statements within the meaning of Section 21E of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, based on the beliefs of the company, as well as assumptions made by, and information currently available to, Enterprise's management team. Although management believes that the expectations reflected in such forward-looking statements are reasonable, it can give no assurance that such expectations will prove to be correct.
Please refer to our latest filings with the SEC for a list of factors that may cause actual results to differ materially from those in the forward-looking statements made during this call. With that, I'll turn it over to Jim.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Thank you, Libby. We had another solid quarter, both in terms of volume and cash flow. We reported adjusted EBITDA of $2.4 billion, compared to $2.2 billion the same quarter last year. We generated $1.8 billion of distributable cash flow. We had 1.6x coverage for the quarter. We retained $661 million of DCF in Q2, and we're at $1.5 billion year to date. Even though Q2 can be seasonally our weakest quarter, our company handled a near record 12.6 million barrels per day of crude oil equivalent volumes and 2.2 million barrels a day of marine terminal volumes, as well as record natural gas processing, and record NGL pipeline and fractionation volumes.
Our investments to support growth in the Permian Basin are visible both volumetrically and financially in our NGL pipeline and service segment, which reported a 19% increase in gross operating margin compared to Q2 of last year, primarily attributable to our four new natural gas processing plants in the Permian and our 12th NGL fractionator at our Mont Belvieu area complex. In addition, we also benefited from improvements in natural gas processing margins compared to last year. Our natural gas pipelines and service segment also reported a 23% increase in gross operating margin compared to the same quarter in 2023. This increase was primarily driven by higher transportation revenues and higher marketing margins associated with the wider spreads between Waha and higher valued market hubs. We had a very good quarter in spite of the challenges of our PDH plants.
They've been somewhat of a headwind throughout the year. We recently completed our turnaround at PDH 1. Planning for the turnaround took over a year and involved a dedicated turnaround team in addition to field engineering and maintenance personnel. This team documented every issue we've had with this plant and developed solutions for each one. The turnaround took 100 days. A few factoids. The turnaround was over 1.25 million hours worked. At the peak, we had 1,250 people per shift. We had 590 work packages executed, 17 million pounds of catalyst handled, 1,465 crane lifts, 198 eighteen-wheeler deliveries. 52,800 bricks hand inspected, over 41,000 replaced. Those bricks are the catalyst support and the catalyst reactor.
The plant is now up and running, and it's exceeding its nameplate. PDH 2 is currently in turnaround. We expect it to be producing PGP sometime around mid-August. The PDH 2 turnaround is not nearly as involved as PDH 1. I'd like to thank our Mont Belvieu team and our supporting service providers for their long hours and hard work during these back-to-back turnarounds. We're confident that these two plants will be a tailwind the rest of the year. We also completed our diluent open season on the TE Products Pipeline. We closed the open season with 100,000 barrels a day of new and recontracted commitments, and I think those are 5-year deals. We then can accommodate this incremental demand with a suite of debottlenecks and horsepower additions while ensuring we do not, it will impact our existing customers.
Finally, our company has $6.7 billion of projects under construction that provide visibility to future earnings and cash flow growth. These projects include three processing plants, one in the Midland Basin, two in the Delaware and associated gathering, our Bahia NGL pipeline, Frac 14, and export expansions at the Neches River Terminal and the Ship Channel. All of these projects are backed by long-term contracts and significantly enhance what is already a very strong NGL value chain. As has been the case for several years running, we continue to see even more rich gas volumes coming from the Permian than we had previously forecasted. Tony may give something on this in the Q&A. With that, I'll turn it over to Randy.
Randy Fowler
Co-CEO and CFO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
All right. Thank you, Jim. Good morning, everyone. Starting with the income statement, net income attributable to common unit holders was $1.4 billion or $0.64 per unit for Q2 2024. This was a 12% increase over Q2 2023. Our adjusted cash flow from operations, which is cash flow from operating activities, on the cash flow statement before changes in working capital, this number increased 11% to $2.1 billion for Q2 2024 compared to $1.9 billion for Q2 2023. We declared a distribution of $0.525 per common unit for Q2 2024. This is a 5% increase over the distribution declared for Q2 2023.
The distribution will be paid on 14 August to common unit holders of record as of the close of business tomorrow, 31 July. In the Q2, the partnership purchased approximately 1.4 million common units off the open market for $40 million. Total purchases for the 12 months ending 30 June 2024 were $176 million, or approximately 6.5 million Enterprise common units. This brings total repurchases under our buyback program to approximately $1 billion or about 50% of the total program amount.
In addition to buybacks, our distribution reinvestment plan and employee unit purchase plan purchased a combined 6.3 million common units on the open market for $171 million during the last 12 months, including 1.8 million common units on the open market for $50 million during Q2 2024. For the 12 months ending 30 June 2024, Enterprise paid out $4.4 billion in distributions to limited partners. Combined with the $176 million of common unit purchases over the same period, Enterprise's payout ratio of adjusted cash flow from operations was 55%. Total capital investments in Q2 2024 were $1.3 billion, which included $1 billion for growth capital projects and $245 million for sustaining capital expenditures.
While our expected growth capital expenditures for 2024 did not change, as a result of the LPG export announcement we announced this morning, we did refine the bottom of our range. Our current estimate of growth capital expenditures for 2024 is now in a range of $3.5 to 3.75 billion. We continue to expect 2025 growth capital investments to be in the range of $3.25 to 3.75 billion. 2024 sustaining capital expenditures are elevated due to planned turnarounds for our PDH 1 plant, our iBDH facility, and our high purity isobutylene facility. These turnarounds typically occur every three to four years.
We now estimate 2024 sustaining capital expenditures to be approximately $600 million, up from $550 million, primarily due to higher capital costs associated with the turnaround at the PDH 1 facility, which was completed in June. The turnaround at the PDH 2 facility began in late June 2024, and as Jim noted, we anticipate completion in the middle of August. As of 30 June 2024, our total debt principal outstanding was approximately $30.6 billion. Assuming the final maturity date for our hybrids, the weighted average life of our debt portfolio was approximately 18 years. Our weighted average cost of debt was 4.7%, and approximately 95% of our debt was fixed rate. Our consolidated liquidity was approximately $3.4 billion at the end of the quarter, including availability under our credit facilities and unrestricted cash.
Our adjusted EBITDA was $2.4 billion for Q2 and $9.7 billion for the 12 months ending 30 June 2024. As of June 2024, our consolidated leverage ratio was 3.0x on a net basis when adjusted for the partial equity treatment of our hybrids and reduced by the partnership's unrestricted cash on hand. Our leverage target remains 3.0x ± 0.25x. With that, Libby, I think we can open it up for questions.
Libby Strait
Senior Director of Investor Relations, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Thank you, Randy. Operator, we are ready to open the call for questions from our participants.
Operator
As a reminder, to ask a question, you will need to press star one one on your telephone. To remove yourself from the queue, you may press star one one again. We ask that you please limit yourself to two questions or one question and one follow-up. Please stand by while we compile the Q&A roster. Our first question comes from the line of Theresa Chen of Barclays.
Theresa Chen
Managing Director, Midstream and Refining Equity Research, Barclays
Morning. Thank you for taking my questions. Maybe starting with the LPG export. So on that front, you've executed and announced multiple expansions, with another one just today. Can you just help us think about what inning are we in terms of export expansion buildup for the industry? Across your system, you know, how much more brownfield capacity expansion do you have left?
Tug Hanley
SVP, Hydrocarbon Marketing, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Yeah. The market's obviously calling for additional capacity. We announced that expansion this morning around call it 85% to 90% contracted of our existing and expansion capacity. As far as our brownfield capacity, we have additional opportunities to execute that. This project was using existing infrastructure. Concerning our term contracts, we're out there with highly competitive rates. You know, like I said, we have additional brownfield opportunities ahead of us.
Theresa Chen
Managing Director, Midstream and Refining Equity Research, Barclays
Okay. Brent, if you can just, you know, help us think about, like, from a commercial perspective, what is the going rate for brownfield expansion across your system, maybe on a per gallon or other unit basis, and how does that compare with greenfield expansions for anyone wanting to get into this part of NGL value chain right now?
Tug Hanley
SVP, Hydrocarbon Marketing, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Teresa, this is Tug talking, but I won't get into a specific rate, but relative to Greenfield, it's significantly more competitive.
Theresa Chen
Managing Director, Midstream and Refining Equity Research, Barclays
Okay. Thank you, Tug. As a follow-up, do you have an update on the commercialization of SPOT at this point?
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Yeah, this is Jim. I'll take that. Yeah, we've you know, up until now, what we've been marketing is a concept, and since we've gotten our license to construct, we're marketing a real project now. We've done a heck of a lot of work to determine how competitive we are versus a single lightering and multi-lightering. If you look at the single lightering, we tracked 563 ships that were single lightering. Out of those 563 ships, we put it into quartiles, and we were hands down better than 280 ships of those and competed very effectively with the first two quartiles. In the multi-lightering, we looked at over 400 ships, and we beat those hands down across the board.
Randy Fowler
Co-CEO and CFO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
If you looked at all the ships we tracked, we tracked 969 ships, and we beat hands down 686 ships of those ships over that timeframe. Now we're gonna see if the market wants it.
Theresa Chen
Managing Director, Midstream and Refining Equity Research, Barclays
Thank you so much.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Michael Blum of Wells Fargo.
Michael Blum
Managing Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Wells Fargo Securities
Thank you. Good morning, everyone. Just wanted to go back to the LPG export discussion a little bit. I wonder if you can just refresh us on what you're seeing for end market demand as you continue to expand capacity. I guess I'm particularly interested in if you're seeing a lot of that incremental demand coming from China. Thanks.
Tug Hanley
SVP, Hydrocarbon Marketing, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Yeah, this is Tug. The demand equation is, you know, obviously important to our LPG export expansions. Fundamentally, at the end of the day, the barrel has to clear the US and the barrel will price accordingly to do so. With respect to China, right now our exports stand around 43% going to China, but we're also
You know, around call it 21% to the Americas and 13% to Europe. We're seeing robust demand across the board.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Doug, is that LPG?
Tug Hanley
SVP, Hydrocarbon Marketing, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
That's LPG.
Michael Blum
Managing Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Wells Fargo Securities
What percentage of LPG goes to China?
Tug Hanley
SVP, Hydrocarbon Marketing, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Around 43%.
Michael Blum
Managing Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Wells Fargo Securities
Propane butane.
Tug Hanley
SVP, Hydrocarbon Marketing, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
propane butane.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Okay. PDH plants. Okay.
Michael Blum
Managing Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Wells Fargo Securities
Great. No, I appreciate that. And then I just wanted to revisit in the capital allocation discussion around buybacks. I think we all understand at this point that, you know, Enterprise, your definitely preferred method of returning cash is distribution growth over buybacks. I'm wondering if you can just refresh us on the criteria where you decide to allocate capital to buybacks, especially given that it seems like you have a pretty nice slate of organic growth opportunities at attractive returns. Thanks.
Randy Fowler
Co-CEO and CFO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Yeah, Michael, this is Randy. Yeah, Mike, what we've been, you know, targeting, you know, over the last few years, and 2024 is not that different, is probably coming in and doing buybacks in the $200 million range. What that's done is, you know, we do issue equity as a component of compensation. When you come in and take a look at what we issue in terms of compensation and what we buy back, you'll see over the last four years, there's a decrease in the number of overall units outstanding. You know, I think that's our focus.
Once we get back out, you know, this year and next year, again, you know, we're talking this year growth capital expenditures in the $3.5 to 3.75 billion range. Growth CapEx next year, we're still estimating at $3.25 to 3.75 billion. That's probably going to keep those buybacks in that $200 million range. Once we get back out to 2026, you know, there we're thinking growth CapEx could be, call it, around $2.5 billion. Then I think we have more room to return capital. I think we really just need to get some visibility on 2026 to see what form that increase in a return of capital would look like as far as distributions and buybacks.
Michael Blum
Managing Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Wells Fargo Securities
Great. Thanks, Randy.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Jeremy Tonet of J.P. Morgan.
Jeremy Tonet
Executive Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, JPMorgan
Hi, good morning. Hello, good morning.
Randy Fowler
Co-CEO and CFO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Good morning, Jeremy.
Jeremy Tonet
Executive Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, JPMorgan
Just wanted to make sure you could hear me there. Thank you. Just wanted to see, I guess, you know, there's been some of your midstream peers out there have been acquiring assets. There's been some bolt-ons and, I just want to, you know, get your thoughts about Enterprise's role within industry consolidation at this point and wanted to see, you know, I guess, any thoughts you could share on that at this point, if this is the last major wave of consolidation in midstream.
Randy Fowler
Co-CEO and CFO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Okay, Jeremy, I'll take first crack at that and from a strategic standpoint, I'll let Jim comment. But I think our first and foremost, what we're looking at is returns on capital and what gives us the best returns on capital and growing cash flow per unit. 'Cause at the end of the day, that's what's gonna drive value. We've taken a look at a number of opportunities, more asset acquisitions than I would say public company M&A. But you know, what we've seen thus far is organic growth is providing us good opportunities at good returns on capital, relatively better returns on capital and in growing cash flow per unit. Obviously, the Navitas deal that we did, that also provided good returns on capital, good cash flow growth.
That's really where our focus is.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Yeah. Strategically, I think we've always said it kind of has to fit what we already have. You know, we talked about the plants we're building in the Permian. I don't think we're through building plants. I like you know, it's got to be the price has got to be right. It's got to fit who we are. When you build a plant, you can put it where it fits who we are. I like the organic side, but we look at everything that comes along. We have more investment bankers come in here than you can say grace over.
Jeremy Tonet
Executive Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, JPMorgan
Got it. Makes sense there. Just wanted to also, I guess, get your thoughts as it relates to power in Texas overall. We've seen, you know, instability in the ERCOT market and other issues out there. Just wondering how you feel about that going forward. Could there be room for your own generation or other measures to kind of ensure, I guess, stability?
Graham Bacon
EVP and Coo, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
This is Graham. I'll take that. Yeah, certainly power in Texas can be a challenge, and it evolves consistently. We're doing things with our projects to basically do some hedging of that through purchase of power generation and looking at other options. We work very closely with the power providers and their status, and evaluate whether grid power will be acceptable or if we need to have either backup power or other power sources available. Each situation is different, every provider is different, whether you're working out in West Texas or East Texas. Each situation is individual.
Jeremy Tonet
Executive Director and Senior Equity Research Analyst, JPMorgan
Got it. Makes sense. I'll leave it there. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Tristan Richardson of Scotiabank.
Tristan Richardson
VP and Equity Research Analyst, Scotiabank
Hi, good morning, guys. Just on Bahia, can you give a general update on progress there and maybe how you see utilization ramping as that project comes on? Maybe just your updated thoughts on a base case for Seminole based on what you're seeing on the supply growth side.
Justin Kleiderer
SVP, Pipelines and Terminals, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Yeah, Tristan, this is Justin Kleiderer. I mean, I think updates on Bahia is we're still on track from a timing perspective. From a commercial perspective, I think go back a couple of quarters how we sort of talked strategically about it, and that is, it's, you know, the growth is underpinned by our GMP platform, which Jim just spoke to. The fact that we don't think we're done building plants, so Bahia will be there to catch those volumes. When you think about NGL pipelines, you have to also understand the totality of the system that feeds them, in which we think we have a premier system with all the connectivity to a majority of the third-party plants that have supply that can feed the system as well.
You really have to look at plant connectivity to really understand what capacity and utilization could look like. Third, we always have the sort of optionality that all of our pipelines give us in terms of potential conversions and things like that. With respect to Seminole, I think it's a prime candidate for repurposing. I think we've been public with that, in which case, if that happens, those NGLs will feed into Bahia.
Tristan Richardson
VP and Equity Research Analyst, Scotiabank
Great. Thank you. Maybe just a clarification question. Sorry if I missed this, but could you talk about the EHT expansion you announced this morning and the 300,000 barrels a day versus maybe what you had talked about previously in that capital slide for EHT? I think you guys referred to it as facility upgrades versus an outright expansion. Can you maybe talk a little bit about the distinction there?
Justin Kleiderer
SVP, Pipelines and Terminals, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
I mean, we're adding an additional refrigeration unit there, expanding the existing dock infrastructure. We're utilizing existing dock infrastructure and pipeline infrastructure that's ultimately getting us to 300,000 barrels a day.
Zach Strait
SVP, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
This is Zach. The original project that was on there was more of a flexibility project between different commodities, which this new train ends up providing.
Tristan Richardson
VP and Equity Research Analyst, Scotiabank
Great. Thank you guys very much. Appreciate it.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Spiro Dounis of Citi.
Spiro Dounis
Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Citi
Thanks, operator. Hey, team. First question just on CapEx, but really kind of want to focus on what's uncommitted at this point. Obviously, SPOT's a big one, and you've mentioned a few times now, the potential for more processing plants to get built. As you think about the rest of the system, you've obviously got plenty of pipeline, plenty of export expansion, obviously some fracs in there. Curious if you could give us a sense of what you think is still missing from that system or maybe areas where customers are coming to you, like with this export expansion and demanding more.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Yeah, I remember Dan one time. This is Jim. Told me, we were looking at something, and he said, "You know, this might be the last deal, Jim." They keep coming at us. I think we are doing a pretty good job of expanding our primary petrochemical product system, meaning our ethylene system and our propylene system. I think we'll be surprised in the years to come how good we'll do in that. I mean, I don't think we have enough export capability based on what I see coming at us in the future. We believe that rich gas out of the Permian is gonna be a couple of 3 Bcf/day more than we have forecasted in the past. We're on that export train.
Spiro Dounis
Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Citi
Gotcha. I guess that does tie to my second question a bit. Just thinking about producers here, curious, maybe this one's for Tony on how you think about the outlook or what happens next. Curious, have you seen any change in behavior? Obviously, seeing gas kind of turn over here a little bit again, and crude, of course, has kind of come off the highs. Are producers acting differently yet? Just curious how you're seeing maybe the next call medium term.
Tony Chovanec
EVP of Fundamentals and Commodity Risk Assessment, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Yeah. Spiro, this is Tony. You know, Jim mentioned in his prepared remarks, I guess, first of all, we don't see significant changes in producers. In other words, there is a lot of money on the tables for producers to continue to produce because of price of oil and how profitable they are. Frankly, they get more profitable every day. While certainly none of them can't like very weak prices at Waha, that doesn't keep them from putting barrels on the table. Jim, in his remarks, mentioned that rich gas continues the trend of exceeding both ours and producers' expectations. What I'd like to add to that is, you know, with Natalie's team, we spend a lot of time with commercial people, producers, and technical people.
In those meetings with producers, we're definitely discussing incremental rich gas over and above, frankly, the type curves that we have in our forecast. I think there's a number of reasons for this, but to boil it down, I think it boils down to some of the richer gassier benches now being drilled and planned by producers, especially in the Delaware Basin. Plus some of the GOR increases that we're predicting driven by the multi-bench completion methods, whatever you wanna call them, that continue to evolve. When we talk about that in our analyst meeting, you know, Natalie always reminds me that we wanna be directionally correct in our forecast. No forecast is correct. But without talking to y'all about what we're seeing, again, in these commercial and technical meetings, I think our...
From directionally correct, I think we'd be lacking. Jim, I think you mentioned two to three incremental Bs. I would say that's over and above the approximately 30 Bs of which rich gas of 20/30 that we had in our forecast. When you look at a basin producing that much gas, you think, well, that's not really a big number. But when you consider the fact that it's liquid rich and as rich as it is, it gets to be a pretty big number pretty quick. So that's the reality of what we're dealing with. Anybody else wanna add anything? Natalie, you agree?
Natalie Gayden
SVP, Natural Gas, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Yeah. The only thing I'd add is, when you think about that much incremental rich gas and more efficient plants in the basin that are capable of extracting higher ethane than before, it becomes a very quick NGL growth number also. One thing that I think has surprised people to the upside is the NGL production out of the basin. Prices have started to do it. The capability of the plants and the portfolio of processing plants now there in the Permian just is much greater than in the past.
Spiro Dounis
Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Citi
Got it. I'll leave it there. Thanks as always.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Keith Stanley of Wolfe Research.
Keith Stanley
Director and Equity Research Analyst, Wolfe Research
Hi, good morning. Following up on the Houston LPG export project, is this a sign that you're perhaps seeing more demand for phase two at the Neches River project to be all ethane instead of a mix of ethane and propane? You have to do the Houston project to accommodate the propane side. Can you just give an update on how much of the Neches River capacity is contracted at this point on both phases?
Tug Hanley
SVP, Hydrocarbon Marketing, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Sure. This is Tug. You're exactly right. We will maintain the flexibility at the Neches River facility to do LPG. However, as the VLEC order book continues to get delivered out between now and, call it, end of 2026, that facility will be in ethane service long term. As far as the contract level we have on that facility, it is 100% contracted. I will tell you, we have additional debottlenecking projects that we can execute fairly capital efficient to get additional capacity there if the market asks for it. We're in good discussions around that capacity right now, and we'll evaluate if we proceed with that. Yeah, I could see it being ethane long term. What was the second question?
Keith Stanley
Director and Equity Research Analyst, Wolfe Research
Great. Thank you. Second question, any kind of a technical one, but just any ability for the company to benefit from the wide isobutane to butane spreads that we've seen, or is the focus really still just MTBE to butane?
Tug Hanley
SVP, Hydrocarbon Marketing, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
We benefit from that spread.
Keith Stanley
Director and Equity Research Analyst, Wolfe Research
From the isobutane to butane?
Tug Hanley
SVP, Hydrocarbon Marketing, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Yes.
Keith Stanley
Director and Equity Research Analyst, Wolfe Research
Got it. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of John Mackay of Goldman Sachs.
John Mackay
VP and Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Hey, everyone. Good morning. Thanks for the time. I wanna go back to, I think maybe it was Michael's question on China. We're seeing at least oil demand kind of trending decently below expectations right now. I guess I'd just be curious to hear from your perspective kind of where demand is trending overall versus your forecast, your expectations on maybe when that could start to pick up. Maybe just how sensitive your outlook could be to that global demand picture, acknowledging the high contracting levels. Thanks.
Tug Hanley
SVP, Hydrocarbon Marketing, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
This is Tug. I'll pass it over to Tony. As far as Enterprise's exports to China is around 43%. The US is around 52%, so we're a little bit lower than the US average. I will add that our product does go to China. It's all indirect, so we don't have any direct contract exposure per se on the LPG side. We are seeing it, you know, ramp up quarter-over-quarter. Then Tony, I'll-
Tony Chovanec
EVP of Fundamentals and Commodity Risk Assessment, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Yeah. If you talk about other liquids demand, and you know, Tug is referencing the barrels going to China, that's. We all know. We've been watching the build-out of PDHs in China for the last three years, and it's nothing short of eye-popping. They dominate the olefins market in Asia at this point, especially relative to PDH activity. So it's really important in the equation. If you're also referring to oil demand, I will tell you from our view, there's nothing wrong with oil demand globally. Probably on track to be growth somewhere between 1.2 million barrels to 1.4 million barrels a day year on year. That's not a bad number, you know, especially with China demand, the somewhat weak economies.
I think other forecasters will tell you the same, that that's about the trajectory we're on.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
This, Jim, I don't think we can undersell the benefits that LPG has with places like Africa and India as a transition fuel from wood and coal. What we're seeing is that's a lot stickier demand, and it doesn't go away.
Tony Chovanec
EVP of Fundamentals and Commodity Risk Assessment, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
In that regard, for those of you who want to search the internet for TotalEnergies' recent commercial that they have been running specifically on LPG in Africa, it's a pretty moving commercial.
John Mackay
VP and Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
I appreciate all that. Thanks. I might push for just one more. I mean, looking ahead to November, you know, tariffs are obviously front of mind. Are those coming up in your commercialization discussions, either around kind of incremental NGL sales or, maybe on spot?
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
What? Say the question again. I'm sorry.
Tug Hanley
SVP, Hydrocarbon Marketing, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Tariffs. Export tariffs.
John Mackay
VP and Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
I guess if we're talking about the risk of incremental tariffs,
Tony Chovanec
EVP of Fundamentals and Commodity Risk Assessment, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
It gets-
John Mackay
VP and Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Say, starting next year, if that's having any impact on commercialization?
Tony Chovanec
EVP of Fundamentals and Commodity Risk Assessment, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
It gets brought up occasionally, but I'll tell you the truth. If you were to ask me that question two years or three years ago, four years ago, especially at the later days of when Trump was in office, it was brought up quite often. We've been over to Asia a couple times this year. Those questions and those conversations don't happen near the frequency that they once did.
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
What does happen, Brent, after the LNG pause? Can I depend on the US? Aren't you getting some of that?
Tony Chovanec
EVP of Fundamentals and Commodity Risk Assessment, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Yeah. I mean, I think people question in terms of what projects are real and if we're gonna continue to expand the export capabilities of this country. I think obviously the people that have contracts in place at the incumbent assets benefit. But in terms of trying to expand anything that they have, especially over in Asia, I think you know that makes them pause if they can continue to grow and depend on the US. But the tariff side, again, I'll just expand on that. On the tariff side, you know, I think we fundamentally believe that if the US product has to price to export, then ultimately the US price has to overcome that tariff based on just pure geography and the transit that they have to incur.
I mean, that's probably more of a reflection of what happens to the US price.
John Mackay
VP and Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
That's fair. I appreciate all the thoughts today. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Neal Dingmann of Truist.
Neal Dingmann
Managing Director, Energy Research, Truist Securities
Morning, all. Thanks for the time. My first question, I always appreciate that capital project slide. I'm just wondering, something you've mentioned earlier kind of got my attention. Just wondering, is it fair to say, you won't spend future CapEx until, you know, it's largely contracted? Or maybe say it another way, wondering if you have a, you know, an amount that needs to be contracted or percent of volumes that need to be contracted before FID or CapEx is spent?
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Really kind of depends on the project, if you wanna know the truth. On PDH, we wanted to make sure we had every bit of that contracted and turned into an annuity. If we see a lot of upside, we'll probably take less of a contract need because we see upside on the asset. It really depends on the asset. For example, on SPOT, I'm not gonna tell you what it is, but we know what we have to have contracted in order to build it.
Neal Dingmann
Managing Director, Energy Research, Truist Securities
That makes a lot of sense. Thanks, Jim. Just one follow-up. Quarter to date, the marketing margin continue to look quite strong, and I'm just wondering, with about a third of Q3 now in the books and Waha prices remaining still quite volatile, I think were anything from $1.50 to -2, just any update you would give on that marketing margin. Thank you.
Brent Secrest
EVP and CCO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Yeah. This is Brent. So from Enterprise's perspective, our number is still the same. We have about $380 million a day of exposure. We've hedged a small amount for the balance of this year, but by and large, we still have a lot of exposure to all the gas markets that originate from Waha.
Neal Dingmann
Managing Director, Energy Research, Truist Securities
Perfect. Thanks, Brent.
Brent Secrest
EVP and CCO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Yes, sir.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Manav Gupta of UBS.
Manav Gupta
Senior Equity Analyst, UBS
Hi, this is Manav from UBS. My first question is, can we talk a little bit about the CapEx creep that happened in 2024? What were the drivers of this? Could this repeat in 2025? Do you have confidence that, you know, this will not happen in 2025?
Randy Fowler
Co-CEO and CFO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
I think we would come in and say, we really didn't see CapEx creep in 2024. We did modify the range. That's why we gave the market an upper range. The lower part of the range changed, but the upper part of the range is still $3.75 billion. Where we sit currently, we're still, you know, 2025, we still feel good about a range of $3.25 to 3.75 billion.
Manav Gupta
Senior Equity Analyst, UBS
Okay. In terms of PDH 2, you get it up in August, so should we assume it runs like at full rates by September? Or do you think it's more of like you get to the full rate in Q4?
Jim Teague
Co-CEO, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
I'm looking at Graham, and I'm expecting to run up at full rates in September. We should be at full rates in September.
Manav Gupta
Senior Equity Analyst, UBS
Okay. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. As there are no further questions in queue, I would now like to turn the conference back to Libby Strait for closing remarks. Madam.
Libby Strait
Senior Director of Investor Relations, Enterprise Products Partners L.P.
Thank you to our participants for joining us today. That concludes our remarks. Have a good day.
